script.text: Would Ukraine withdraw from the Donbas, if it could join NATO? Volodymyr Zelensky says that is what U.S. negotiators asked him this week. He says it is the first time membership has been tied to land.

Five stories, ranked by impact. From petrol stations in Russia, to a pipeline across the Saudi desert, to a room in China where three nuclear powers plan to meet. And at the end, the one condition Kyiv calls its absolute minimum.

Number five: Russia's fuel. Two industry sources told Reuters on Tuesday that Ukrainian drone strikes since late October have disrupted about thirty percent of Russia's oil refining capacity. Nine of the thirty-five largest refineries were affected, they said. The estimate is based on nameplate capacity, and it has not been officially confirmed. The plants hit since late October can process about three hundred thousand tonnes of crude a day, out of a national total of about nine hundred thirty thousand. On Monday, the governor of the Leningrad region said a drone attack set the Kirishi refinery on fire. Kirishi is Russia's second largest. Overnight into Wednesday, the same governor said one hundred forty-six drones were downed over his region, and a fire broke out in the port zone of Ust-Luga, on the Baltic Sea. Reuters could not verify the drone count. Across the border, Lithuania and Latvia told residents to take shelter, according to reports. For Russian drivers, the effect is direct. Euronews and Semafor report that Rosneft, the country's biggest oil company, now limits fuel sales in several regions, to thirty litres per purchase in cities. Rosneft had eased those limits in October, during a pause in the strikes. The current figure is still below the peak. In September, Ukraine's military claimed more than forty-five percent of Russian refining had been knocked out. Next: the oil routes around Hormuz.

Number four: the oil routes around Hormuz. On Thursday, Iran's Revolutionary Guards said two supertankers were disabled by explosions on what Tehran calls an unauthorised route in the south of the strait. Iran's army said two more tankers hit mines. The ships were not named, and Reuters could not verify the Iranian account. The same day, Yemen's Houthis claimed attacks on a second oil route. Their spokesman, Yahya Saree, said a drone hit Pumping Station Number Seven on Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline, and that a ballistic missile targeted an oil facility in the Red Sea port of Yanbu. He also claimed a drone strike on an Aramco building in Riyadh. Saudi Arabia did not confirm any damage. The Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted two drones, one over the Riyadh region and one over the Eastern Province. So why does this pipeline matter? It is Saudi Arabia's way around Hormuz. Reuters reports the kingdom is sending about four million barrels of crude a day through it, from the oil fields in the east to Yanbu on the Red Sea. Markets reacted. Brent crude, the benchmark for much of the world's oil, settled up three point three percent on Thursday, at ninety-five dollars and eighty-two cents a barrel. Even so, it was still down for the week. Crude prices feed into what drivers pay at the pump. Next: a war declared over, and a strait that stays shut.

Number three: a war declared over, and a strait that stays shut. Quick question. When did the war that shut the Strait of Hormuz begin? Take a guess. On February twenty-eighth, with U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran. Since then, Tehran has demanded that ships get its permission to pass, Arab News reports. On Monday, after meeting Qatar's prime minister at the White House, President Trump said the war is militarily effectively over. He said the United States would keep the status quo and hold off new strikes, Al Jazeera reports. But according to CBS News, he also warned that American forces are locked and loaded. And the U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports stays in place. Reuters reports what Iran is offering. A halt to U.S. bombing, eased sanctions and an end to the blockade, in return for reopening Hormuz, with nuclear talks to follow. Iran's foreign ministry says Tehran will keep its commitments if the blockade and sanctions are lifted. Security official Mohsen Rezaei says Washington must first accept Iran's seven conditions. Qatar says the talks continue. By Thursday, Trump wrote that the United States no longer needs a deal with Iran, CNBC reports. About a fifth of the world's oil normally passes through this strait, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration. Next: three leaders, one room.

Number two: a summit with no precedent. On Friday, the White House said Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin plan to meet together on the sidelines of the APEC summit in Shenzhen, in southern China. Reports put the meeting on Thursday, November nineteenth, at the end of Trump's visit to China. Turkey's Anadolu agency reports that the Kremlin has named the same date. AP calls the meeting unprecedented. On the agenda, according to the White House: nuclear weapons and the Iran war. New START, the last treaty capping American and Russian strategic warheads, expired in February. A senior U.S. official said China's arsenal is growing fastest, and that Beijing should join arms control talks. Here is the scale. The Federation of American Scientists estimates Russia has about five thousand four hundred sixty warheads, the United States about five thousand one hundred eighty, and China about six hundred. Together, that is more than nine in ten of the world's nuclear weapons. But no deal is expected. U.S. officials call the meeting a starting point. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov calls it extremely significant. Beijing only says it is in contact with the other sides, and it has long refused three-way nuclear talks. No separate Trump-Putin meeting is planned, the U.S. official said. Next: a trade nobody had floated before.

Number one: Ukraine, and a question that redraws the map. On Tuesday and Wednesday, American mediators brought Russian and Ukrainian delegations together in Abu Dhabi. Both sides confirmed an agreement in principle on a large prisoner exchange. Russia's state agency TASS says it should happen within two to three weeks. On a ceasefire and on territory, there was no breakthrough, U.S. mediators said. Russia still demands all of the Donetsk region, according to reports, and Kyiv rejects that. Ukraine's negotiator David Arakhamia called it one of the toughest rounds so far. On Thursday, envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner met Vladimir Putin in Moscow. Putin told them that foreign peacekeeping troops in Ukraine would be treated as a continuation of the war, reports say. Then came Zelensky's account, published on Saturday. He says the American side asked: what if Ukraine joins NATO? Would Ukraine then withdraw from the Donbas? Al Jazeera reports the areas in question are ones Russia does not control. Zelensky says Ukraine will not hand over land, or recognise occupied areas as Russian. But with a full package, security guarantees, a strong army and money to rebuild, he would put the question to Ukrainians in a referendum. Washington has not confirmed the idea. Kushner says only that several new ideas emerged and are being explored, and that NATO will remain a critical pillar of European security. No Kremlin reaction has been reported. Moscow has long rejected NATO membership for Ukraine. Membership would put Ukraine under the alliance's mutual defence clause, the one that already covers most of Europe.

What happens next. On Thursday, the three leaders are due in Shenzhen, and U.S. officials expect no agreements there, only a starting point. The prisoner exchange from Abu Dhabi is due within weeks, according to TASS. On Iran, the blockade and Tehran's conditions both remain, while Qatar keeps mediating. On the Donbas idea, the sides set out the paths themselves. Zelensky says he would only put it to a referendum with the full package. A U.S. official told the BBC that many proposals are still under discussion, and that any final deal needs both Ukraine and Russia to agree. And Moscow has long said no to Ukraine in NATO. So what is the one condition Kyiv calls its absolute minimum? Security guarantees like NATO's Article Five, Zelensky said in the same remarks. Article Five is the clause that says an armed attack against one member shall be considered an attack against them all. Will Ukraine hold a referendum on the Donbas within a year? Tell us in the comments: yes or no.
Next Wednesday: NATO's Article Five. What does an attack on one really oblige the allies to do, and what would it mean for Ukraine?

upload.title: Donbas for NATO? This Week's 5 Biggest Stories
upload.description:
The five biggest geopolitical stories of November 9 to 15, 2026: Ukraine's drone strikes on Russian oil refineries and Rosneft's fuel limits, Iranian claims of tanker attacks in the Strait of Hormuz and Houthi claims of strikes on Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline and Yanbu, Trump calling the Iran war militarily over while the U.S. blockade and Hormuz closure continue, the planned Trump–Xi–Putin meeting at APEC in Shenzhen, and the Abu Dhabi Russia–Ukraine talks, the prisoner swap deal and Zelensky's account that U.S. negotiators floated Ukraine leaving the Donbas in exchange for NATO membership. Every claim is attributed to the source that reported it; unverified claims are labelled as such.
